newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy to grow 2.5 pct in 1997 - UCLA study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy to grow 2.5 pct in 1997 - UCLA study.

text.p: The U.S. econony should grow around 2.5 percent next year, with no apparent threat of inflation, according to a quarterly study released Wednesday by economists at the University of California Los Angeles.

The UCLA study said real gross domestic product will continue to grow moderately next year and inflation will remain low, with consumer prices rising 2.8 percent in 1997. Producer prices are expected to rise only one percent in 1997.
The economists said the moderate rate of inflation is not expected to put pressure on the Federal Reserve Bank to be aggressive when it comes to interest rates.

On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve opted to hold interest rates steady, leaving the key federal funds rate that commerical banks charge each other for overnight loans at 5.25 percent and the discount rate that the Fed charges banks for money at 5.0 percent.

The UCLA study said corporate pre-tax profits are expected to perk up to a six percent growth rate next year, compared with a modest three percent increase in 1996. However, that is still down from the 13 percent growth experienced in 1995.
The growth rate for business fixed investment will remain at around 6.3 percent in 1997, about the same as in 1996, but down from 9.5 percent in 1995.
Housing starts will average around 1.48 million units in 1997, almost the same as this year's starts of 1.47 million. The effective mortgage rate is expected to fall to 7.22 percent in 1997.

Real consumer spending for goods and services is expected to grow at 2.4 percent next year, slightly below the real GDP growth. Unemployment is expected to fall by 0.2 percent next year to 5.2 percent and then perk up to 5.3 percent in 1998.
